title: Trust structure critical in new tax regime
full_text:
SMSFs invested in a unit trust must ensure that vehicle is fixed in nature to avoid paying the minimum 30 per cent tax proposed for discretionary trusts, a legal expert has noted.
DBA Lawyers lawyer Fraser Stead stated the new tax regime, which was announced in this year’s federal budget, would not apply to complying superannuation entities, such as SMSFs, nor to fixed trusts, but a fund may be forced to pay the impost as a result of an investment in a unit trust.
To illustrate the impact of such an investment, Stead gave the example of two funds, the Dean SMSF and the Fred SMSF, which are equally invested in a unit trust. The Dean SMSF has a single member who is receiving a pension, which accounts for 100 per cent of his fund’s assets, while the Fred SMSF has only accumulation entitlements.
The income for the 2029 financial year for the trust is $200,000 and each SMSF receives $100,000 in trust distributions, which is their only income, and since the trust is not fixed, the minimum 30 per cent tax will apply.
“How does this actually work for SMSFs from 1 July 2028? The first thing we work out is the trustees’ minimum tax. We have $200,000 in income and applying a 30 per cent tax rate equals $60,000,” Stead noted.
“Fred has ordinary and statutory income of $100,000 because he has $0 of exempt income since everyone’s in accumulation.
“The SMSF pays 15 per cent and the fund will receive a half share of the non-refundable minimum tax offset, so it gets 50 per cent of the offset.
“This means there is no tax payable for Fred because $15,000 minus $30,000 is going to leave us with zero tax.
“The issue is we have $15,000 of wasted offset the trust paid that is not going to be recouped at the beneficiary level by the SMSF.
“For Dean, it’s worse. He has $100,000, but his SMSF has 100 per cent exempt current pension income and that means he has no taxable income.
“So the $30,000 – his share of the beneficiary non-refundable offset – is going to be completely wasted.
“In total, the trust pays $60,000 in tax, but $45,000 of that is not recouped at all by the beneficiaries.
“This is why, for SMSFs investing in unit trusts, it’s really important to make sure that the trust is fixed under the new definition [in these laws].
“Accumulation entitlements, pension entitlements and things like non-arm’s-length income will determine what the impact is of having a unit trust that’s not fixed.
“What do you do instead of this? Get the unit trust varied or make sure it is fixed where you have SMSF investors because there is good potential for wasted tax offsets where an SMSF is invested in a unit trust.”
author: Jason Spits
heading: Superannuation and Investments
